title: Tomb Autobiographies
short: Officials told their lives in set phrases: "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked."
trouble: Students read these lines as personal confessions. They are partly ideal statements of a good life.

blocks.html: From the Old Kingdom on, officials carved accounts of their lives on tomb walls and stelae. They are called autobiographies, though they follow conventions as fixed as those of the offering formula. Their grammar is the jw + sḏm.n=f of jw sḏm.n=f in Narrative, line after line.

A set phrase of many autobiographies: jw rdj.n=j t n ḥqr ḥbs n ḥꜣy "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked". Others: ḏd.n=j mꜣꜥt jr.n=j mꜣꜥt "I spoke what is right and did what is right". These are ideal statements of a good life, not personal confessions.

A tomb was a public place. Visitors were asked to read the offering formula aloud for the owner, and the owner's claim to deserve it was his life lived by maat, right order. So he set down the deeds that maat required: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, speaking truly, harming no one. Because every good official claimed the same virtues, the same phrases recur from tomb to tomb. Some autobiographies add real events too, such as journeys and royal favors; Harkhuf of Aswan, for example, describes his expeditions to the south.

blocks.title: Read the line
blocks.q: Translate jw rdj.n=j t n ḥqr ḥbs n ḥꜣy.
steps: jw introduces a statement; rdj.n=j "I gave".
t n ḥqr "bread to the hungry"; the verb is not repeated for the second pair: ḥbs n ḥꜣy "clothes to the naked".
ḥqr and ḥꜣy are adjectives used as nouns: "the hungry one", "the naked one".
blocks.a: "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked."

blocks.title: Parse a verb
blocks.q: What form is jr.n=j in jr.n=j mꜣꜥt?
steps: The eye jr: the stem of jrj "do".
.n then =j: the sḏm.n=f, completed action.

blocks.html: Breasted's Ancient Records of Egypt (1906) translated many of these texts; his version of Harkhuf's lines reads "I gave bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked". The wording is old-fashioned in places, but the phrase is the one you have just read.

Reading these lines as personal confessions or as a diary. They are partly an ideal portrait, the life every official was expected to have led, written in the phrases everyone used. That does not make them false; it means they tell us first what Egyptians valued. Check: if the same sentence appears in other tombs, read it as a convention.
